title: Deadlock Avoidance

answers: Both workers lock in one order
writing.exampleCaption: Sorting by id gives every transfer the same first lock, so two transfers cannot wait on each other.
writing.explanation:
Rust prevents data races, not deadlocks. A consistent order for acquiring multiple locks and avoiding calls into unknown code while locked remove common wait cycles.

A deadlock can arise when worker A holds lock X while waiting for Y and worker B holds Y while waiting for X. Both workers may be perfectly data-race-free, yet neither can move. Rust's ownership rules do not decide a global lock order for your program. The simplest prevention is often a consistent acquisition order: if every path takes X before Y, the cycle cannot form from those two locks.

Draw a wait-for graph with one node per task and an arrow when it waits for a resource held by another task. A cycle is the warning sign. Reduce the number of locks held at once, move expensive work outside locked sections, or combine related fields under a single mutex when the data model allows it. `try_lock` can avoid indefinite waiting in some designs, but a retry loop without backoff can livelock or waste CPU. Timeouts help detection and recovery; they do not automatically make a transfer atomic.

Build two workers that each need two locks. First write the unsafe ordering on paper, then rewrite both workers to acquire locks in the same order. Ask what happens if a callback called while holding X attempts to acquire X again: a non-reentrant mutex may self-deadlock. Avoid invoking unknown callbacks while a guard is alive. When reviewing a codebase, document the lock hierarchy near the shared state, not only in one caller. Tests can expose some schedules; a clear acquisition rule is the stronger argument that a cycle cannot occur.
writing.feedback: Both workers take `X` before `Y`, so neither can hold `Y` while waiting for `X`, and that cycle cannot form.

recall.question: Why is replacing `lock()` with a loop of `try_lock()` retries not automatically a deadlock fix?
recall.answer: Without backoff, threads can keep failing and retrying in step (livelock) and burn CPU, and progress still isn't guaranteed. A timeout or `try_lock` helps detect contention; it doesn't make a two-lock transfer atomic. A consistent lock order is the stronger fix.

recall.question: Why is calling an unknown callback while holding a `MutexGuard` risky?
recall.answer: The callback might lock the same mutex; `std::sync::Mutex` is not re-entrant, so the thread waits on itself and deadlocks. It might also take other locks in a different order. Drop the guard, or copy the needed data out, before calling unknown code.
